title: This ER Doctor Became a Hospital’s First Clinical AI Engineer
description: When Boston Children’s Hospital posted a job listing for a prompt engineer in 2023, Dinesh Rai decided to apply. He didn’t expect to get the job. At the time, prompt engineering was being touted as one of the hot new jobs created by generative AI. Companies wanted people who knew how to coax the best answers from large language models (LLMs) by carefully wording instructions, supplying examples, and giving the systems personas or other context. Dinesh Rai Employer: Boston Children’s Hospital Occupation: Clinical AI Engineer Education: Bachelor’s degree in supply-chain management and marketing sciences, Rutgers Business School; Doctor of Medicine, Albert Einstein College of Medicine It was an unusual role for a hospital, but Rai had an unusual résumé. While he was trained as an emergency physician, he had also taught himself to code just before entering medical school. After completing a fellowship in clinical informatics—which focuses on the intersection of clinical practice and IT systems—he moved into health technology. Boston Children’s brought him on board in August 2023. Three years later, Rai still works there. Prompt engineering, however, has become a much less important part of the job . When he joined, the expectation was that prompting would become a job in itself. “Knowing how to prompt AI properly was going to be the job function of the future,” says John Brownstein , chief innovation officer at Boston Children’s. Early on, the hospital needed internal expertise about how to begin using AI, Brownstein says. Now, better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems—and determining whether its answers can be trusted. Brownstein says the questions they focus on these days have shifted: “How do you embed these tools in your day-to-day operations? How do you build agents to manage literally everything that you do?” For Rai, that has meant embracing a job broader than the role that brought him to Boston. “I’m more like a clinical AI engineer now,” he says. Between medicine and engineering Rai originally studied business as an undergraduate and began teaching himself to code in 2014 (the same year he entered medical school), as neural networks and image recognition were starting to attract wider attention. He kept building software while training as a doctor. In medical school, for instance, he created a platform called Academius for students to track residency interviews and assemble their rank lists. For Rai, the appeal of coding was its scale. In emergency medicine, he could make a direct difference for the individual patient in front of him. Software offered the possibility of building something that thousands of clinicians might use for many more patients. His 2021–22 informatics fellowship made the possibility of doing that full-time feel real. In 2022, Rai took a job at Pieces , a health care AI company, where he led work to bring LLM-based medical summarization into clinical use. That meant taking a break from practicing medicine altogether. “Stepping away was definitely a hard decision,” Rai says. But he wanted to give the technology work his full attention. He has since reactivated his medical license and hopes to return to clinical practice in some capacity within the next year. At Boston Children’s, roughly half his day now looks like an engineer’s: working with developers, writing code, and advancing projects from the technical side. The other half is spent with clinicians, figuring out what they actually need. That combination has become the point of the job. Uncovering “clinical doppelgangers” One project, called clinical doppelgangers , is designed to help doctors treating complicated patients find similar cases buried in the hospital’s historical data. Medical guidelines are generally based on large populations, but at a hospital that handles rare and complex diseases, an individual child may not fit neatly into the populations represented in published studies. The system is being developed to let clinicians identify previous patients with relevant similarities, examine their trajectories, and see how different interventions turned out. It is not meant to replace randomized clinical trials. Instead, it could provide another source of evidence when a physician is facing a case for which the published literature offers little guidance. Projects like that require more than knowing how to ask an LLM the right question. They require understanding what hospital data means, how a clinician will use an answer, and how an AI system can go wrong. Rai recently encountered some of those challenges while working on another project with a clinical team and a development team. They were deciding how much of a patient’s medical record to give an AI model when asking it to identify findings relevant to a particular clinical outcome. Better models have made elaborate prompting less important, so the harder work is building AI into actual health care systems. Both groups initially favored giving the model access to more information, but for different reasons. The developers assumed any data point could be useful. The clinicians assumed the model would recognize irrelevant findings and ignore them. Rai saw a problem with both assumptions. Clinically, an abnormal lab result or vital sign is not necessarily relevant to the question being asked. And from a technical perspective, an LLM cannot be counted on to recognize that irrelevance. If the system asks the model whether a given abnormality matters, it may construct a plausible explanation for why it does, even when the record does not support the connection. “That’s where the dual perspective has been valuable,” Rai says, “not just translating between teams, but recognizing when an approach that looks reasonable from either perspective rests on assumptions we shouldn’t make.” After the prompt In medicine, the challenges surrounding the prompt are now more important than polishing the prompt itself. Is the model’s output consistent with the underlying data? How should its results be evaluated? Will the clinician using it be able to recognize a mistake? That also means listening to clinicians’ experience. For the platform Rai’s team built to draft clinical notes, the clinicians who would go on to use the tool reviewed a batch of generated notes before anything was finalized. Someone who had cared for a complicated patient in the cardiac intensive care unit for weeks would catch an error far more easily than someone skimming the chart afterward, Rai says. Although AI adoption in medicine is surging, some health care professionals still have concerns about its use . “I think some skepticism is healthy, and we don’t try to talk people out of it,” he says. The team told clinicians up front that it was a generative AI tool meant to support their judgment, not replace their own review of the chart. “People trust it more when they’ve seen its mistakes than when we just tell them it’s good.” An evolving career The evolution of Rai’s role reflects how quickly AI-focused jobs can change, so Rai is wary of telling people interested in careers like his to master any particular tool. For people who want hands-on engineering jobs, fundamental programming skills still matter . Some understanding of machine learning is useful, as is experience building and testing systems. But not every clinician who wants to work with AI needs to become a database architect or take a deep dive into algorithms. What Rai considers indispensable is domain knowledge. In the medical field, that means understanding how health care workflows operate, how electronic health record data is created, what that data actually represents, and where care breaks down. That may be the more durable lesson from a career that briefly carried one of AI’s buzziest job titles. “The value isn’t just knowing how to get an answer from a model,” Rai says. “It’s knowing what context it needs and whether that context supports the answer we’re asking it to give.”

title: How Engineers Designed a Mission to One of Jupiter’s Icy Moons
description: On 3 December 2026, a 30.5-meter-wide space probe will slingshot past Earth, picking up the speed it needs to reach Jupiter in 2030. The Europa Clipper is designed to investigate Jupiter’s enigmatic moon Europa and look for places that could support life in the ocean beneath the moon’s thick shell of ice. Tim Larson is the project manager for the mission at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, and he spoke to IEEE Spectrum about designing and flying the Europa Clipper . Tim Larson Tim Larson is the project manager for NASA’s Europa Clipper mission. He has been at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif., for over 35 years. Why take such a roundabout route to Jupiter? Tim Larson: That’s all driven by the energy that we got from our launch vehicle, the Falcon Heavy . It set a MEGA trajectory: Mars-Earth Gravity Assist. So about 4 months after launch, we flew by Mars, got an assist there. Now we’re coming back in for a final assist from Earth to get on our outbound trajectory to Jupiter. The Europa Clipper is set to orbit Jupiter and fly by Europa about 50 times to study it. Why not just orbit it directly? Larson: The big challenge is the radiation environment. It is so intense that any spacecraft orbiting Europa wouldn’t last very long. So the mission designers came through with this concept of the flybys. We will be in a three-week orbit around Jupiter, but the orbit is synchronized so that every time we fly by Jupiter, Europa is right there. Over time, you build up the coverage of the surface that we’re ultimately after. We spend a relatively short time in the high-radiation environment, and then the rest of the orbit is in a more benign environment where we can relay data back down to Earth, et cetera. The Europa Clipper relies on solar panels to generate power. Why not use a compact radioisotope thermoelectric generator (RTG)? Larson: It’s a national policy to only use RTGs if it is absolutely essential. A lot of the early concepts that focused on orbiting Europa had to go with RTG approaches, because you’d spend so much time in the shadow of Jupiter. Once we shifted over to the flyby mission approach, it turned out solar arrays would be feasible. How are Europa Clipper ’s electronics different from other probes? Larson: One of the things that we dealt with in our design was the level of radiation tolerance that we had to get in all our parts. In our main avionics module—we call it the vault —everything in there is designed to an exposure of 150 kilorads (1,500 sieverts ). To get our usual factor-of-two margin , we were buying parts that rated to 300 kilorads. That brings up side challenges, because when you buy high-radiation-tolerance versions of parts, you can’t always get the exact same part functionality. You might have to change your circuits a little bit. And they don’t always have the same form factor, so you have to accommodate that. How do you preserve fine-grained technical knowledge about the spacecraft over its yearslong mission lifetime? Larson: By the time we launch, we try to get everything documented. As we learn about the idiosyncrasies of the spacecraft, we capture that in databases. When we have personnel turnover, we try to have a lot of overlap. We’re looking at how AI can take in this broad array of information we have in multiple different formats and locations, and extract information. This article appears in the December 2026 print issue as “Tim Larson.”

title: Mitsubishi Electric Research Lab CEO on How He Reached the C-Suite
description: The trajectory from researcher to top executive at a leading R&D organization doesn’t happen overnight. It took Anthony Vetro nearly 30 years to climb the corporate ladder at Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories , in Cambridge, Mass. He joined MERL in 1996, right out of college, and he has worked there ever since. Vetro probably is best known for his research in multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression. Anthony Vetro Employer Mitsubishi Electric Research Laboratories, in Cambridge, Mass. Title President and CEO Member grade Fellow Alma mater Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school) He became an IEEE Fellow in 2011 for his contributions to video coding, three-dimensional television, and multimedia adaptation. Mitsubishi Electric has moved away from making televisions. It now focuses on developing systems including ones used for defense, electronics, the energy industry, and space exploration. His ascension up the executive ranks began in 2018, when he was named a vice president and director of MERL. In 2023 he was appointed its president and CEO. He also works closely with the company’s new U.S.-based innovation facility in Cambridge. And he recently took on a dual role as deputy head of Mitsubishi Electric’s global R&D activities, including in Asia and Europe. Vetro credits IEEE with helping him develop his management skills after he served in several IEEE Signal Processing Society leadership positions. He also learned from his key roles in establishing international standards for digital image formats and video compression, he says. “Between my IEEE activities, standards work, and some of the business shifts in Mitsubishi Electric, I eventually graduated to more management leadership roles,” he says. A multimedia pioneer Vetro is the son of immigrants. His father came to the United States from Italy and his mother from Sweden when they were both in their early 20s. They settled in New York City, on Staten Island. Although neither parent went to college, his father stressed the importance of education to his son at an early age. “My father started in the mailroom and worked his way up to eventually managing communication accounts and infrastructure for large financial companies,” he says. “My mother worked in banks, first as a teller and later doing bank reconciliation after pursuing some professional certifications. “Through their jobs, they saw people with college degrees getting better positions and promotions, so education was something really ingrained in me.” Vetro says he developed a passion for mathematics and engineering in middle school. He was accepted into the Staten Island Technical High School , a specialized pre-engineering institution. There he solidified his interest in pursuing a career in the field. “A lot of students didn’t know what they wanted to major in at college, but I knew fairly early,” he says. He was accepted into the accelerated bachelor’s and master’s engineering degree programs at the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school ). He began his bachelor’s degree program in 1992 and the master’s program in 1994. “As part of the master’s degree program, I needed to do a thesis,” he says. “I wasn’t sure exactly what it would be on. Soon after taking my first course on image processing, I was certain that was an area I wanted to work in.” It was an interesting time, he says, because broadcast television was going through a major transformation, shifting from analog to digital during the early 1990s. It was long before streaming services, he notes. “I feel that industry-level engagement in IEEE is very vital to the organization in maintaining high relevance in the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity.” “The idea of being able to come up with compact ways to represent this very rich information was really appealing to me,” he says. “I’m also a visual learner. I liked seeing images, and there was some nice math behind them, too.” After he earned both degrees in 1996, Mitsubishi Electric hired him for its technical staff. He conducted research on multimedia signal processing, focusing on video compression. “The opportunity to work on projects around digital TV broadcasting and image processing attracted me,” he says. He conducted research in video conferencing, Internet and mobile streaming, and video coding technology, widely used for broadcasting, DVDs, and Blu-ray discs. He developed several technologies including digital TV receivers and displays, surveillance and camera-monitoring systems, automotive equipment, and satellite imaging systems. Another advantage of joining the company, he says, was that it allowed him to pursue a doctorate in electrical engineering, also from Polytechnic, while working. “That really sealed the deal,” he says. He received the degree in 2001. The road to management After six years as a technical staff member, he was promoted in 2007 to manage the group working on digital video coding, processing, and streaming. Seven years later, Vetro became its deputy director, a top-level management position that he held until 2018. “After working for about 10 years exclusively on video compression processing technology, there were some shifts in our company’s business. Its overall strategy began to change,” he says, “so I became interested in broadening my experience beyond video.” He was asked to lead the lab’s speech and audio team. It was more development-oriented, he says, and focused on vehicle infotainment and speech interfaces before Alexa and Siri existed. He pivoted the team’s focus more toward research and established strategic paths tailored to emerging opportunities within the organization. Recognizing emerging trends in sensing and information security, he formed groups that worked on them. Mitsubishi Electric’s first U.S. innovation hub To help spur innovation between Mitsubishi Electric and its U.S. customers, the company in June opened Serendie Street Boston , its first digital transformation hub in the United States. It’s colocated with MERL. The new office is modeled after the first Serendie Street collaboration space, which Mitsubishi Electric launched in 2024 in Yokohama, Japan. The word serendie is a combination of serendipity and digital engineering , according to the company’s website . Serendie is the digital platform designed to foster collaborations between data, people, and technology, it says. The space where people interact to extract ideas from the data is called “the street.” The platform brings together researchers, startups, customers, and partners to identify new products, test them, run pilot programs, and scale them up. Vetro says he’s excited about the endeavor. “Serendie Street [Boston] aims to strengthen the bridge between our global R&D efforts and real-world industry challenges. The hub is intended to bring our partners and customers together to engage in more cocreation activities, where we listen to their problems and work together to solve them,” he says. “I think the company has come to recognize that we can’t just do it all internally by ourselves.” The technologies being worked on include robotics, energy solutions such as integrating renewable energy into the grid, and more energy-efficient data center systems . The decision to colocate the hub with MERL offices was deliberate, Vetro says. “The area has a very rich ecosystem,” he says. “We have Harvard , MIT , and many other universities a stone’s throw away.” Strengthening IEEE’s involvement with industry Vetro joined IEEE in 1992 as a student member during an event the Polytechnic’s student branch was holding. He enjoyed reading the IEEE Potentials student member publication and other periodicals, he says. “In the earliest stages of my career, IEEE was a place where I could attend conferences, read journals, and stay on top of the latest research and trends,” he says. “Over the years, I was able to build a professional network, which has been helpful. That facilitated a lot of research collaboration with university professors attending the conferences. “In more recent years, IEEE has provided a great platform for industry to exhibit thought leadership and discuss real-world problems we’re facing. I think these discussions may have even set some research directions among the academic community.” Vetro is an active volunteer for the IEEE Signal Processing Society . He has chaired several of its technical committees and conferences, and he served as an associate editor for some of its journals. He says he’s most proud of establishing the society’s industry board and serving as its inaugural chair. The board formed a corporate engagement program , launched the Industry Signals newsletter, developed short courses tailored to industry, and holds career fairs at the society’s flagship conferences . Vetro also had a hand in MERL sponsoring two IEEE technical field awards : the Flanagan Speech and Audio Processing Award and the Fourier Award for Signal Processing . “Industry-level engagement in IEEE is really very vital to the organization in maintaining its relevance to the community and fulfilling its mission of fostering technological innovation and excellence for the benefit of humanity,” he says.
